promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.

learningObjectives.title: 5.5 Rotational Equilibrium and Newton’s First Law in Rotational Form
5.6 Newton’s Second Law in Rotational Form

questions.q: A turbine starts from rest at t = 0. Its angular acceleration is α = α₀(1 − t/T) for 0 ≤ t ≤ T and zero for t > T, where α₀ and T are positive constants. Through what angle does the turbine turn from t = 0 to t = 2T?
optionWhy: A student who thinks zero angular acceleration means the turbine is at rest picks this: only the first stage counts, α₀T²/3. After T, α = 0 means only that ω stops changing; the turbine keeps turning at α₀T/2.

Integrating α from rest gives ω = α₀(t − t²/(2T)), so by t = T the turbine has turned α₀T²/3 and reached ω = α₀T/2. After T, α = 0 means ω stays at α₀T/2, which adds α₀T²/2 over the next interval T. Total: (5/6)α₀T² ≈ 0.83 α₀T².

A student who multiplies the angular velocity at t = 2T, α₀T/2, by the whole interval 2T picks this: α₀T². During the first stage ω was less than α₀T/2, so the turbine turned through less than (α₀T/2)T then.

A student who uses the first stage's average angular acceleration, α₀/2, in θ = ½αt² picks this: ¼α₀T² for the first stage plus α₀T²/2 afterward. Because α is largest early, ω grows faster at first than a constant α₀/2 would make it, and the first-stage angle is α₀T²/3, not α₀T²/4.
questions.explain: Integrating α from rest gives ω = α₀(t − t²/(2T)), so by t = T the turbine has turned α₀T²/3 and reached ω = α₀T/2. After T, α = 0 means ω stays at α₀T/2, which adds α₀T²/2 over the next interval T. Total: (5/6)α₀T² ≈ 0.83 α₀T².
questions.working: For 0 ≤ t ≤ T: ω = ∫₀ᵗ α₀(1 − t′/T) dt′ = α₀(t − t²/(2T)), so ω(T) = α₀T/2, and θ(T) = ∫₀ᵀ ω dt = α₀(T²/2 − T²/6) = α₀T²/3. For T < t ≤ 2T: α = 0, so ω stays α₀T/2 and the turbine turns a further (α₀T/2)(T) = α₀T²/2. Total: α₀T²/3 + α₀T²/2 = (5/6)α₀T² ≈ 0.83 α₀T². Distractors: α = 0 taken to mean at rest after T, α₀T²/3 ≈ 0.33 α₀T²; ω at t = 2T multiplied by the whole interval, (α₀T/2)(2T) = 1.00 α₀T²; average angular acceleration α₀/2 in θ = ½αt² for the first stage, ¼α₀T², plus α₀T²/2, = 0.75 α₀T². Key and distractors checked with sympy.

questions.q: The graph shows the angular position θ of a wheel as a function of time t, with three points marked on it. Which ranking of the wheel's angular speeds |ω₁|, |ω₂| and |ω₃| at points 1, 2 and 3 is correct?
optionWhy: A student who reads the height of the θ–t graph as the angular speed picks this, ranking 8 rad > 5 rad > 2 rad. The angular speed is the steepness of the graph, not its height.

A student who uses θ/t, the slope of a line from the origin, picks this: 2 rad/1 s = 8 rad/4 s = 2 rad/s, and 5 rad/7 s ≈ 0.7 rad/s. θ/t is the average angular velocity since t = 0; the angular speed at a point is the slope of the tangent there.

A student who compares signed slopes picks this, putting point 3's negative slope last. At point 3 the wheel is turning back, but faster than at point 2: angular speed is |ω|, so the sign does not make it smaller.

Angular speed is the magnitude of the slope of the θ–t graph. The graph is steepest at point 1, falls moderately steeply at point 3 and is nearly flat at point 2, close to the top of the curve, so |ω₁| > |ω₃| > |ω₂|.
questions.explain: Angular speed is the magnitude of the slope of the θ–t graph. The graph is steepest at point 1, falls moderately steeply at point 3 and is nearly flat at point 2, close to the top of the curve, so |ω₁| > |ω₃| > |ω₂|.
questions.working: Angular speed is the magnitude of the slope of the θ–t graph. From tangent lines: about +3 rad/s at point 1, about +0.5 rad/s at point 2 (close to the maximum) and about −1.5 rad/s at point 3. So |ω₁| > |ω₃| > |ω₂|. (Heights: 8 rad > 5 rad > 2 rad gives 2, 3, 1. θ/t: 2 rad/1 s = 8 rad/4 s = 2 rad/s > 5 rad/7 s. Signed slopes: +3 > +0.5 > −1.5.)

questions.q: The graph shows the angular velocity ω of a disk as a function of time t, with counterclockwise taken as positive. What is the disk's angular displacement from t = 0 to t = 9 s?
optionWhy: A student who adds all the areas as positive picks this: 30 rad + 4 rad = 34 rad, the total angle turned. From 7 s to 9 s the disk turns clockwise, so that area subtracts.
The angular displacement is the signed area under the ω–t graph. Above the axis, from 0 to 7 s: 6 + 18 + 6 = 30 rad. Below the axis, from 7 s to 9 s: −4 rad. So Δθ = 30 rad − 4 rad = +26 rad.
A student who leaves out the area below the time axis picks this. From 7 s to 9 s the disk turns clockwise through 4 rad, which reduces the angular displacement to 26 rad.
A student who multiplies the final angular velocity by the whole time picks this: −4 rad/s × 9 s = −36 rad. ω changes throughout, so Δθ must be found from the area under the graph.
questions.explain: The angular displacement is the signed area under the ω–t graph. Above the axis, from 0 to 7 s: 6 + 18 + 6 = 30 rad. Below the axis, from 7 s to 9 s: −4 rad. So Δθ = 30 rad − 4 rad = +26 rad.
questions.working: Δθ is the signed area between the graph and the t-axis. 0–2 s: (1/2)(2 s)(6 rad/s) = 6 rad. 2–5 s: (3 s)(6 rad/s) = 18 rad. 5–7 s: (1/2)(2 s)(6 rad/s) = 6 rad. 7–9 s: (1/2)(2 s)(−4 rad/s) = −4 rad. Δθ = 6 + 18 + 6 − 4 = +26 rad. (Magnitudes added: 34 rad. Area above the axis only: 30 rad. Final ω × 9 s: −36 rad.)

questions.q: A wheel of radius R starts from rest and turns about a fixed axle with constant angular acceleration α. The magnitude of the acceleration of a point on the rim at time t is Rα multiplied by which factor?
optionWhy: The rim point has a tangential component a_T = Rα and, since ω = αt, a centripetal component a_c = Rω² = Rα²t². These are perpendicular, so a = √(a_T² + a_c²) = Rα√(1 + α²t⁴).
A student who takes a_T = Rα as the whole acceleration picks this. The point also moves on a circle with ω = αt, so it has a centripetal component, Rα²t², that grows with time.
A student who takes ω at time t to be θ/t = αt/2 gets a_c = R(αt/2)² = Rα²t²/4 and a = √((Rα)² + (Rα²t²/4)²) = Rα√(1+α²t⁴/16). The angular velocity at time t is αt, so a_c = Rα²t².
A student who adds the magnitudes of the two components picks this: Rα + Rα²t². The components are perpendicular, so they combine as √(a_T² + a_c²).
questions.explain: The rim point has a tangential component a_T = Rα and, since ω = αt, a centripetal component a_c = Rω² = Rα²t². These are perpendicular, so a = √(a_T² + a_c²) = Rα√(1 + α²t⁴).
questions.working: Tangential component: a_T = Rα. ω = αt, so the centripetal component is a_c = v²/R = Rω² = Rα²t². They are perpendicular: a = √((Rα)² + (Rα²t²)²) = Rα√(1 + α²t⁴). (Tangential only: Rα. ω taken as θ/t = αt/2: a_c = Rα²t²/4, a = Rα√(1 + α²t⁴/16). Magnitudes added: Rα(1 + αt²).) The factor multiplying Rα is √(1 + α²t⁴).

questions.q: The figure shows a rigid disk rotating about a fixed axle at O, and two points on it, P and Q, at the distances from O shown. Which gives the ratios of the angular velocities and of the linear speeds of Q and P?
optionWhy: A student who thinks all points of the disk move at the same speed picks this; ω = v/r then makes Q's angular velocity half of P's. The points share one angular velocity, and it is their speeds that differ.
A student who thinks a point farther out rotates faster, in proportion to r, picks this; v = rω then gives v_Q = (2r)(2ω_P) = 4v_P. Every point of a rigid disk has the same ω, so v_Q/v_P = 2.
All points of a rigid disk turn through the same angle in the same time, so ω_Q = ω_P. Speed is v = rω, and Q is twice as far from O as P, so Q moves twice as fast.

A student who thinks every point of a rigid disk moves in exactly the same way picks this. The points share ω, but Q, twice as far from O, travels twice as far in each turn, so its speed is twice P's.
questions.explain: All points of a rigid disk turn through the same angle in the same time, so ω_Q = ω_P. Speed is v = rω, and Q is twice as far from O as P, so Q moves twice as fast.
questions.working: All points of a rigid disk share ω, so ω_Q/ω_P = 1. v = rω, so v_Q/v_P = (2r)/r = 2.

questions.q: A student watching a spinning fan claims: 'A point at the tip of a blade has a greater angular velocity than a point near the hub, because the tip moves faster.' Which statement correctly evaluates the claim?
options: Incorrect: both points turn through the same angle in any time, so they share one ω.
Correct: the tip moves faster, and a point that moves faster turns at a greater ω.
Incorrect: the point near the hub has the greater ω, since its r in ω = v/r is smaller.
Correct: ω and speed are the same quantity, so the faster tip has the greater ω.
optionWhy: The blade is rigid: a straight line along it stays straight as it turns, so the tip and the point near the hub sweep through the same angle in any time and share one ω. The tip moves faster because v = rω and its r is larger.
A student who thinks a point that moves faster must rotate faster picks this. Speed depends on the distance from the axis as well as on ω: the tip moves faster only because it is farther out.
A student who thinks every point of the blade moves at the same speed picks this; ω = v/r is then larger near the hub. The points share one ω, and the tip's speed is greater because v = rω.
A student who thinks angular velocity and linear speed are the same quantity picks this. They are related by v = rω; the faster tip has a larger r, not a larger ω.
questions.explain: The blade is rigid: a straight line along it stays straight as it turns, so the tip and the point near the hub sweep through the same angle in any time and share one ω. The tip moves faster because v = rω and its r is larger.

questions.q: A uniform rod of mass M and length L is held horizontal and can rotate about an axle through a point L/4 from its left end. What is the magnitude of the torque exerted on the rod by the gravitational force about the axle? Take g as the acceleration due to gravity.
optionWhy: A student who measures the distance to the center from the rod's left end instead of from the axle picks this: Mg(L/2). Distances for torque are measured from the axle, which is L/4 from that end.

For torque, the gravitational force on the uniform rod is exerted at its center, L/2 from the left end and so L/2 − L/4 = L/4 from the axle. The force is perpendicular to the rod: τ = Mg(L/4) = 0.25 MgL.
A student who places the gravitational force at the far end of the rod, 3L/4 from the axle, picks this. For a uniform rod it is exerted at the center, L/4 from the axle.

A student who splits the rod at the axle and adds the magnitudes of the two parts' torques picks this: (3M/4)g(3L/8) + (M/4)g(L/8) ≈ 0.31 MgL. The two torques are in opposite senses, so they subtract: 0.28 MgL − 0.03 MgL = 0.25 MgL.
questions.explain: For torque, the gravitational force on the uniform rod is exerted at its center, L/2 from the left end and so L/2 − L/4 = L/4 from the axle. The force is perpendicular to the rod: τ = Mg(L/4) = 0.25 MgL.
questions.working: The gravitational force Mg is exerted at the center of mass, L/2 from the left end, which is L/2 − L/4 = L/4 from the axle. The force is perpendicular to the rod: τ = Mg(L/4) = 0.25 MgL. (Distance measured from the left end, L/2: 0.50 MgL. Force at the far end, 3L/4 from the axle: 0.75 MgL. Rod split at the axle and the two torque magnitudes added: (3/4)Mg(3L/8) + (1/4)Mg(L/8) = (10/32)MgL ≈ 0.31 MgL.)

questions.q: The figure shows, seen from above, a flat plate that can rotate about a fixed axle at O, drawn on a square grid, and three forces, F₁, F₂ and F₃, of equal magnitude exerted on it in the plane of the page. Which ranking of the magnitudes of the torques τ₁, τ₂ and τ₃ about O is correct?
optionWhy: A student who uses the distance from O to each point of application picks this: 5 squares for F₁, about 4.1 for F₃ and about 2.2 for F₂. F₃ is exerted far from O, but its line of action passes only 1 square from O.

A student who measures each distance from O along the direction of the force picks this: 4 squares for F₃, 3 for F₁ and 1 for F₂. The lever arm is perpendicular to the force's direction, not along it.

The forces are equal, so the torques rank as the lever arms, the perpendicular distances from O to the lines of action: F₁'s vertical line is 4 squares from O, F₂'s vertical line is 2 squares from O and F₃'s horizontal line is 1 square from O.
A student who thinks equal forces exert equal torques picks this. Torque also depends on the lever arm, which differs for the three forces.
questions.explain: The forces are equal, so the torques rank as the lever arms, the perpendicular distances from O to the lines of action: F₁'s vertical line is 4 squares from O, F₂'s vertical line is 2 squares from O and F₃'s horizontal line is 1 square from O.
questions.working: Lever arm = perpendicular distance from O to each line of action, in grid squares: F₁ is vertical through the point 4 squares left of O, so 4; F₂ is vertical through the point 2 squares right of O, so 2; F₃ is horizontal through the point 1 square below O, so 1. Equal forces, so τ₁ > τ₂ > τ₃. (Distances from O to the points of application: 5, about 2.2 and about 4.1 squares. Distances along the forces' directions: 3, 1 and 4 squares.)

questions.q: A force F⃗ = (6.00î + 1.00ĵ) N is exerted on a rigid object at a point whose position relative to the object's axis of rotation is r⃗ = (0.300î + 0.400ĵ) m. The axis is perpendicular to the xy-plane. What is the magnitude of the torque exerted by the force about the axis?
optionWhy: A student who multiplies matching components and adds, xF_x + yF_y = (0.300)(6.00) + (0.400)(1.00), picks this. That is the dot product r⃗ · F⃗, a scalar; torque is the cross product r⃗ × F⃗.

A student who multiplies the magnitudes, |r⃗||F⃗| = (0.500 m)(6.08 N), picks this, as if the force were perpendicular to r⃗. Only the part of the force perpendicular to r⃗ produces torque, so the angle between the vectors matters.
A student who adds the magnitudes of the two components' torques, 0.300 N·m + 2.40 N·m, picks this. One is counterclockwise and the other clockwise, so they partly cancel: 2.40 − 0.300 = 2.10 N·m.

For vectors in the xy-plane, τ_z = xF_y − yF_x = (0.300 m)(1.00 N) − (0.400 m)(6.00 N) = 0.300 N·m − 2.40 N·m = −2.10 N·m. The y-component tends to turn the object counterclockwise and the x-component clockwise, so their torques partly cancel; the magnitude is 2.10 N·m.
questions.explain: For vectors in the xy-plane, τ_z = xF_y − yF_x = (0.300 m)(1.00 N) − (0.400 m)(6.00 N) = 0.300 N·m − 2.40 N·m = −2.10 N·m. The y-component tends to turn the object counterclockwise and the x-component clockwise, so their torques partly cancel; the magnitude is 2.10 N·m.

questions.q: A student claims that, for rotation in a given plane, any rigid object's rotational inertia is least about the axis through its center of mass. Which reasoning correctly supports the claim?
options: Contributions r² dm on opposite sides of the center of mass cancel, leaving only the unbalanced mass
x_cm is at the object's middle, where its mass is closest to the axis on average
Gravity's torques balance about the center of mass, Σ τ = 0, so it turns most easily there
About a parallel axis a distance d away, I′ = I_cm + Md², and Md² is positive for any nonzero d
optionWhy: A student who thinks contributions from opposite sides of an axis cancel picks this. Every element contributes r² dm > 0, so nothing cancels; the minimum comes from the Md² term, not from cancellation.
A student who identifies the center of mass with the geometric middle picks this. For a nonuniform object they are different points, and the claim is about the center of mass, wherever it is.

A student who mixes up rotational inertia with the torques exerted on an object picks this. Rotational inertia depends only on the mass distribution relative to the axis, not on gravity or any other force.

The parallel axis theorem relates the rotational inertia about any parallel axis to I_cm. Md² can only add to I_cm, and it is zero only when the axis passes through the center of mass, so I_cm is the least value in that plane.
questions.explain: The parallel axis theorem relates the rotational inertia about any parallel axis to I_cm. Md² can only add to I_cm, and it is zero only when the axis passes through the center of mass, so I_cm is the least value in that plane.
questions.working: Parallel axis theorem: I′ = I_cm + Md². Since M > 0 and d² ≥ 0, I′ ≥ I_cm, with equality only for d = 0, the axis through the center of mass.

questions.q: The diagram shows a thin rod of length L whose linear mass density increases along its length as λ = λ₀x/L, where x is the distance from the rod's narrow left end. The rod can rotate about an axis perpendicular to the page through any one of the labeled points. About which point is the rod's rotational inertia least, and why?
options: R, because the rod's center of mass is at x = 2L/3
Q, because it is at x = L/2, the rod's middle
S, because the densest part, at x = L, is then on the axis
Any of them, because the rod and its mass do not change
optionWhy: x_cm = ∫x dm/M = 2L/3, at R. For rotation in a given plane, I is least about the axis through the center of mass: I_R = ML²/18, compared with ML²/12 about Q, ML²/6 about S and ML²/6 about P.

A student who expects the least rotational inertia about the middle picks Q. That holds only when the middle is the center of mass; here more mass is toward S, so the center of mass is at 2L/3 and I_Q = ML²/12 exceeds I_R = ML²/18.
A student who expects the least value when the densest part is on the axis picks S. The rest of the rod is then up to L away: I_S = ML²/6, three times I_R.
A student who treats rotational inertia as a property of the rod alone picks this. Moving the axis changes every element's distance from it, giving values from ML²/18 about R to ML²/6 about P and S.
questions.explain: x_cm = ∫x dm/M = 2L/3, at R. For rotation in a given plane, I is least about the axis through the center of mass: I_R = ML²/18, compared with ML²/12 about Q, ML²/6 about S and ML²/6 about P.
questions.working: x_cm = ∫x dm/M = (λ₀L²/3)/(λ₀L/2) = 2L/3, at R. With M = λ₀L/2: I_end = ∫x²λ dx = ML²/2; I_R = ML²/2 − M(2L/3)² = ML²/18; I_P (L/3) = ML²/18 + M(L/3)² = ML²/6; I_Q = ML²/12; I_S = ML²/6. Least about R.

Four axis positions are marked with dots along the rod and lettered P, Q, R and S. A scale below gives their distances from the left end: P at L/3, Q at L/2, R at 2L/3 and S at L (the wide right end); the scale starts at 0 at the narrow left end.

questions.q: A thin uniform rod of mass 2.0 kg and length 1.2 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to the rod through a point 0.30 m from one end. Using I = ∫ r² dm, what is the rod's rotational inertia about this axis?
optionWhy: A student who subtracts the short piece on the other side of the axis gets λ(0.90³ − 0.30³)/3 = 0.39 kg·m². Every element contributes x² dm, which is positive on both sides of the axis.

Put the origin on the axis: the rod runs from −0.30 m to +0.90 m with λ = 2.0/1.2 kg/m. I = λ∫x² dx = λ(0.90³ + 0.30³)/3 = 0.42 kg·m². The short piece on the far side of the axis adds a positive amount, since x² > 0 there.
A student who measures r from the end of the rod uses the end-axis result ML²/3 = (2.0)(1.2)²/3 = 0.96 kg·m². The axis is 0.30 m in from the end, so the distances must be measured from there.
A student who treats rotational inertia as the same about any axis uses the center result ML²/12 = 0.24 kg·m². The axis is 0.30 m from the center, which adds M(0.30 m)² = 0.18 kg·m².
questions.explain: Put the origin on the axis: the rod runs from −0.30 m to +0.90 m with λ = 2.0/1.2 kg/m. I = λ∫x² dx = λ(0.90³ + 0.30³)/3 = 0.42 kg·m². The short piece on the far side of the axis adds a positive amount, since x² > 0 there.
questions.working: λ = M/L = 2.0 kg / 1.2 m = 1.67 kg/m. With x measured from the axis, the rod runs from x = −0.30 m to x = +0.90 m. I = ∫ x² λ dx = λ[x³/3] from −0.30 to 0.90 = (1.67 kg/m)(0.729 + 0.027)/3 m³ = 0.42 kg·m². (Check: ML²/12 + M(0.30 m)² = 0.24 + 0.18 = 0.42 kg·m².)

questions.q: A uniform beam of mass M and length L hangs horizontally from two vertical strings, one at each end. A block of mass M sits at the center of the beam. The block is moved to a point L/4 from the left end, and the beam stays horizontal and at rest. By what factor does the tension in the left string change?
optionWhy: Take torques about the right string. With the block at the center, T_L = Mg/2 + Mg/2 = Mg. With the block L/4 from the left end, its lever arm about the right end is 3L/4: T_L = Mg/2 + 3Mg/4 = 1.25Mg. The tension increases by a factor of 1.25.

A student who thinks the strings always share the load equally picks this. Moving the block toward the left string increases that string's share: the torque balance about the right end gives T_L = 1.25Mg.

A student who thinks the farther string carries more of the block's weight gives the left string only Mg/4 from the block, so T_L = Mg/2 + Mg/4 = 0.75Mg. The nearer string carries the larger share: 3Mg/4 of the block's weight.
A student who leaves the beam's own weight out of the torque balance compares Mg/2 with 3Mg/4, a factor of 1.5. The beam's weight adds Mg/2 to the tension in both cases, which makes the factor 1.25.
questions.explain: Take torques about the right string. With the block at the center, T_L = Mg/2 + Mg/2 = Mg. With the block L/4 from the left end, its lever arm about the right end is 3L/4: T_L = Mg/2 + 3Mg/4 = 1.25Mg. The tension increases by a factor of 1.25.
questions.working: Torques about the right end: T_L L = Mg(L/2) + Mg(x_R), where x_R is the block's distance from the right end. Center: x_R = L/2, T_L = Mg. At L/4 from the left: x_R = 3L/4, T_L = Mg/2 + 3Mg/4 = 5Mg/4. Factor 1.25.

questions.q: A wheel turns on a fixed horizontal axle that exerts a frictional torque of magnitude 0.50 N·m on it. A block of mass 3.0 kg hangs from a string wound around a drum of radius 0.20 m on the wheel. A second string, wound the opposite way around a drum of radius 0.25 m on the same wheel, is pulled straight down so that the block rises at a constant speed. What is the magnitude of the force pulling on the second string? Use g = 10 m/s².
optionWhy: A student who thinks the force on one string equals the tension in the other picks 30 N. The strings act at different radii and the axle exerts a frictional torque, so the torque balance gives 26 N.

Constant speed means the block's string has tension mg = 30 N, and constant angular velocity means zero net torque on the wheel. The pull's torque must balance both the block's torque and the opposing friction: F(0.25) = 30(0.20) + 0.50, so F = 26 N.
A student who takes the axle's frictional torque to help the rotation gets F(0.25) = 6.0 − 0.50, so F = 22 N. Friction opposes the rotation, so the pull must supply an extra 0.50 N·m.

A student who expects the force at the larger radius to be larger, swapping the lever arms, gets F(0.20) = 30(0.25) + 0.50, so F = 40 N. Each force's torque uses its own radius: the pull acts at 0.25 m and the block's string at 0.20 m.
questions.explain: Constant speed means the block's string has tension mg = 30 N, and constant angular velocity means zero net torque on the wheel. The pull's torque must balance both the block's torque and the opposing friction: F(0.25) = 30(0.20) + 0.50, so F = 26 N.
questions.working: The block moves at constant velocity, so the tension in its string is mg = 30 N. The wheel's angular velocity is constant, so Στ = 0 about the axle: F(0.25 m) = (30 N)(0.20 m) + 0.50 N·m = 6.5 N·m, the frictional torque opposing the rotation. F = 6.5/0.25 = 26 N.

questions.q: The diagram shows a uniform rod of mass M and length L that can turn without friction about a horizontal axle through point P, perpendicular to the page. The rod is held horizontal and released from rest. What is the magnitude of its angular acceleration just after release?
optionWhy: A student who uses ML²/12, the rotational inertia about the center, gets (MgL/4)/(ML²/12) = 3.00 g/L. The rod turns about P, so the parallel axis term M(L/4)² must be added.
A student who uses ML²/3, the result for a pivot at the end, gets (MgL/4)/(ML²/3) = 0.75 g/L. P is not at the end; about P, I = (7/48)ML².
A student who measures the weight's lever arm from the end of the rod, L/2, gets (MgL/2)/((7/48)ML²) ≈ 3.43 g/L. The lever arm is measured from the axle at P: L/2 − L/4 = L/4.
The weight acts at the center, L/4 from P, so τ = MgL/4. About P, I = ML²/12 + M(L/4)² = (7/48)ML². α = τ/I = (12/7)(g/L) ≈ 1.71 g/L.
questions.explain: The weight acts at the center, L/4 from P, so τ = MgL/4. About P, I = ML²/12 + M(L/4)² = (7/48)ML². α = τ/I = (12/7)(g/L) ≈ 1.71 g/L.
questions.working: The center of mass is L/2 − L/4 = L/4 from P, so τ = Mg(L/4). I_P = ML²/12 + M(L/4)² = ML²/12 + ML²/16 = (7/48)ML². α = τ/I_P = (L/4)/(7L²/48) × g = (12/7)(g/L) ≈ 1.71 g/L.

questions.q: A uniform rod pivoted at one end on a frictionless horizontal axle is held horizontal and released from rest. It is replaced by a uniform rod of the same material and thickness but twice as long, which is released in the same way. By what factor does the rod's angular acceleration just after release change?
optionWhy: A student who attends only to the torque, which grows by a factor of 4, picks this. The rotational inertia grows by a factor of 8, so α decreases.

A student who thinks rotational inertia depends only on mass takes I to double while the torque quadruples, giving ×2. The doubled length also puts mass twice as far from the pivot, multiplying I by 8 in all.
Doubling the length doubles the mass. The weight's torque, MgL/2, grows by 2 × 2 = 4; the rotational inertia, ML²/3, grows by 2 × 2² = 8. So α = τ/I changes by 4/8 = ½, consistent with α = 3g/(2L).

A student who reasons that everything falls with the same acceleration picks this. For rotation about a pivot, α = 3g/(2L) depends on the length, so the longer rod's angular acceleration is half as large.
questions.explain: Doubling the length doubles the mass. The weight's torque, MgL/2, grows by 2 × 2 = 4; the rotational inertia, ML²/3, grows by 2 × 2² = 8. So α = τ/I changes by 4/8 = ½, consistent with α = 3g/(2L).
questions.working: Same material and thickness: mass doubles, M → 2M; L → 2L. Torque of the weight about the pivot τ = MgL/2 → ×4. I = ML²/3 → ×2 × 4 = ×8. α = τ/I → ×4/8 = ×½. (α = 3g/(2L) directly.)

questions.q: A wheel is rotating in the positive θ direction as it passes θ = 0. The graph shows the net torque τ exerted on the wheel as a function of its angular position θ. At which position is the wheel's rotational kinetic energy greatest?
options: At θ₁, as beyond θ₁ the torque decreases and so the wheel begins to slow down.
At θ₃, as by then the wheel has turned through the greatest angle under the torque.
Everywhere from 0 to θ₁, as the torque has its greatest value throughout that range.
At θ₂, as the graph's area is positive up to θ₂ and negative beyond it.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a decreasing torque slows the wheel picks this. Between θ₁ and θ₂ the net torque is smaller but still in the sense of rotation, so it still does positive work and the wheel keeps speeding up.
A student who adds all the area under the graph as positive picks this. Beyond θ₂ the torque opposes the rotation, so the area there is negative work and the kinetic energy decreases.

A student who reads the kinetic energy from the height of the graph picks this. The torque gives the rate of energy transfer per radian; the kinetic energy follows the accumulated area, which is still growing after θ₁.

The kinetic energy at any position equals the kinetic energy at θ = 0 plus the net work done since, the area under the τ–θ graph from 0. That area grows while τ is positive, up to θ₂, and shrinks once τ is negative, so the kinetic energy is greatest at θ₂.
questions.explain: The kinetic energy at any position equals the kinetic energy at θ = 0 plus the net work done since, the area under the τ–θ graph from 0. That area grows while τ is positive, up to θ₂, and shrinks once τ is negative, so the kinetic energy is greatest at θ₂.

figure.alt: Graph of net torque τ on the vertical axis against angular position θ on the horizontal axis, with the θ-axis drawn at τ = 0 and the τ-axis extending below it. The horizontal axis is marked θ₁, θ₂ and θ₃. From θ = 0 to θ₁ the torque has a constant positive value. From θ₁ it decreases along a straight line, passing through zero at θ₂ (marked with a dot) and becoming negative, until θ₃. No numerical values are given.

questions.q: A wheel of rotational inertia I starts from rest. The net torque exerted on it depends on its angular position θ as τ = τ₀(1 − θ²/θ₁²), where τ₀ and θ₁ are positive constants, so the torque falls to zero at θ = θ₁. What is the wheel's angular speed at θ = θ₁?
optionWhy: A student who treats the torque as constant at its greatest value, τ₀, picks this: W = τ₀θ₁ and (1/2)Iω² = τ₀θ₁, so ω = √(2τ₀θ₁/I) ≈ 1.41√(τ₀θ₁/I). The torque falls to zero, so the work is ∫τ dθ = 2τ₀θ₁/3, less than τ₀θ₁.
The work done is W = ∫₀^θ₁ τ₀(1 − θ²/θ₁²) dθ = τ₀θ₁ − τ₀θ₁/3 = 2τ₀θ₁/3, the area under the τ–θ curve. Setting (1/2)Iω² = 2τ₀θ₁/3 gives ω = √(4τ₀θ₁/(3I)) = √(4/3)·√(τ₀θ₁/I) ≈ 1.15√(τ₀θ₁/I).
A student who finds the work correctly as 2τ₀θ₁/3 but writes the kinetic energy as Iω² picks this: ω² = 2τ₀θ₁/(3I), so ω ≈ 0.82√(τ₀θ₁/I). With K_rot = (1/2)Iω², ω² = 4τ₀θ₁/(3I).

A student who takes the average torque to be the mean of its values at the two ends, (τ₀ + 0)/2 = τ₀/2, picks this: W = τ₀θ₁/2 and (1/2)Iω² = τ₀θ₁/2, so ω = √(τ₀θ₁/I). The torque does not fall linearly with θ, so its average is (1/θ₁)∫τ dθ = 2τ₀/3, not τ₀/2.
questions.explain: The work done is W = ∫₀^θ₁ τ₀(1 − θ²/θ₁²) dθ = τ₀θ₁ − τ₀θ₁/3 = 2τ₀θ₁/3, the area under the τ–θ curve. Setting (1/2)Iω² = 2τ₀θ₁/3 gives ω = √(4τ₀θ₁/(3I)) = √(4/3)·√(τ₀θ₁/I) ≈ 1.15√(τ₀θ₁/I).
questions.working: W = ∫₀^θ₁ τ₀(1 − θ²/θ₁²) dθ = τ₀θ₁ − τ₀θ₁/3 = 2τ₀θ₁/3. Work–energy: (1/2)Iω² − 0 = 2τ₀θ₁/3 → ω = √(4τ₀θ₁/(3I)) = √(4/3)·√(τ₀θ₁/I) ≈ 1.15√(τ₀θ₁/I). Distractors: W = τ₀θ₁ (torque taken as τ₀ throughout) → √(2τ₀θ₁/I) ≈ 1.41√(τ₀θ₁/I); Iω² = 2τ₀θ₁/3 → √(2τ₀θ₁/(3I)) ≈ 0.82√(τ₀θ₁/I); average torque taken as (τ₀ + 0)/2, W = τ₀θ₁/2 → 1.00√(τ₀θ₁/I).

questions.q: A pulley is a uniform solid disk of mass 4m and radius R that turns on a fixed horizontal axle through its center with negligible friction. A light string is wrapped around the pulley, and a block of mass m hangs from its free end. The block is released from rest, and the string does not slip on the pulley. With g the magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity, how long after release does the pulley's angular speed reach ω₁?
optionWhy: A student who takes the string's tension to be the block's weight, mg, picks this: mgR t = 2mR²ω₁. While the block accelerates downward the tension is less than mg, so the torque on the pulley is smaller and the time is longer.

The disk's rotational inertia is (1/2)(4m)R² = 2mR². Newton's second law for the block, mg − F_T = ma, and for the pulley, F_T R = Iα with a = αR, give a = g/3 and F_T = (2/3)mg. The angular impulse of the string's torque equals the pulley's change in angular momentum: F_T R t = 2mR²ω₁, so t = 3.0ω₁R/g.

A student who treats the block as falling freely, with acceleration g, picks this: the string's speed ω₁R is reached when gt = ω₁R. The string must exert a torque to turn the pulley, so it pulls up on the block and the block's acceleration is less than g.

A student who takes the disk's rotational inertia to be (4m)R², as if all its mass were at the rim, picks this: a = g/5 and F_T = (4/5)mg. A uniform solid disk has I = (1/2)MR² about its central axis, so I = 2mR² here.
questions.explain: The disk's rotational inertia is (1/2)(4m)R² = 2mR². Newton's second law for the block, mg − F_T = ma, and for the pulley, F_T R = Iα with a = αR, give a = g/3 and F_T = (2/3)mg. The angular impulse of the string's torque equals the pulley's change in angular momentum: F_T R t = 2mR²ω₁, so t = 3.0ω₁R/g.
questions.working: Pulley: I = (1/2)(4m)R² = 2mR². Block: mg − F_T = ma. Pulley: F_T R = Iα, with a = αR. So F_T = Ia/R² = 2ma, mg = 3ma, a = g/3 and F_T = (2/3)mg. Rotational impulse–momentum theorem for the pulley (the axle force and the pulley's weight act through the axle): F_T R t = Iω₁ − 0, so t = 2mR²ω₁/((2/3)mgR) = 3.0ω₁R/g. Check with the pulley–block system about the axle: the only external torque is the block's weight, mgR; the system's angular momentum is Iω₁ + m(ω₁R)R = 3mR²ω₁, so mgR t = 3mR²ω₁, t = 3ω₁R/g. Distractors: F_T = mg: mgR t = 2mR²ω₁, t = 2.0ω₁R/g; block falls with acceleration g: gt = ω₁R, t = 1.0ω₁R/g; I = (4m)R²: mg = 5ma, F_T = 4mg/5, t = 4mR²ω₁/((4/5)mgR) = 5.0ω₁R/g.

questions.q: A ball of mass m is thrown horizontally with speed v₀ from point P at the top of a cliff. Air resistance is negligible, and g is the magnitude of the acceleration due to gravity. What is the magnitude of the ball's angular momentum about P at time t after it is thrown, before it lands?
optionWhy: Gravity's torque about P is mg times the horizontal distance v₀t, so it grows linearly from zero. The angular impulse is ∫₀ᵗ mgv₀t′ dt′ = mgv₀t²/2, and since the angular momentum about P is zero at the throw, this is L. The same result comes from |r⃗ × p⃗| = |xp_y − yp_x|.

A student who multiplies gravity's torque about P at time t, mgv₀t, by the whole time t picks this. That torque grows from zero at the throw, so the angular impulse is the area under a rising line, half of mgv₀t².

A student who thinks only spinning objects, or objects moving in a circle, have angular momentum picks this, since the ball neither spins nor circles P. Angular momentum about a point is r⃗ × p⃗, which is nonzero here because the ball's momentum does not point along the line from P.

A student who takes the ball's angular momentum to be its linear momentum, m times its speed √(v₀²+g²t²), picks this. Angular momentum about P is r⃗ × p⃗ and depends on where the ball is relative to P; this expression does not even have the units of angular momentum.
questions.explain: Gravity's torque about P is mg times the horizontal distance v₀t, so it grows linearly from zero. The angular impulse is ∫₀ᵗ mgv₀t′ dt′ = mgv₀t²/2, and since the angular momentum about P is zero at the throw, this is L. The same result comes from |r⃗ × p⃗| = |xp_y − yp_x|.
questions.working: Take P as the origin, x horizontal in the direction of the throw and y upward. At time t: r⃗ = (v₀t, −gt²/2) and p⃗ = (mv₀, −mgt). L_z = xp_y − yp_x = (v₀t)(−mgt) − (−gt²/2)(mv₀) = −mgv₀t² + mgv₀t²/2 = −mgv₀t²/2, so |L⃗| = mgv₀t²/2. Check by angular impulse: the ball starts at P, so L₀ = 0; gravity's torque about P has magnitude mg(v₀t), its lever arm being the horizontal distance v₀t; L = ∫₀ᵗ mgv₀t′ dt′ = mgv₀t²/2. Distractors: (mgv₀t)·t = mgv₀t² (torque at time t times the whole time); 0 (no angular momentum without spin or circular motion); |p⃗| = m√(v₀²+g²t²) (linear momentum taken as angular momentum).
